```{r setup, warning=FALSE}
library(leaflet)
library(leaf.magic)
```

# Purpose

The purpose of `{leaf.magic}` is to extend R `{leaflet}`'s capability to use modern icon sets. While `leaflet::addAwesomeMarkers()` exists, it has a few core disadvantages; markers are a fixed size, can only be one of 19 colours, and pull icons from significantly out of date icon sets.

`{leaf.magic}` takes icons from up-to-date icon libraries - Font Awesome, Bootstrap, Lucide and Ionicons - and nests them inside its own SVG marker shapes, which `leaflet::makeIcon()` then turns into `{leaflet}`-usable map markers.

Some core advantages of `magicIcons()` over `leaflet::awesomeIcons()` are:

* Markers pull from up-to-date, larger icon sets.

* Markers and icons can be any colour, and can be resized. As markers are vector images, they stay sharp at any size and on high resolution screens.

* Markers come in a range of shapes - and you can design your own.

* Icons can be mapped to data with `iconFactor()`, `iconBin()` and `iconQuantile()`, and explained with `addIconLegend()`, just like colours in `{leaflet}`.

Each marker is only built once per R session, so maps with many repeated markers are quick to draw.

# Example Data

In this document we'll use the in-built `port_talbot` dataset, which details the location of some air quality measurement stations around the town of Port Talbot, Wales, UK, some of which are open and some of which have closed.

We can give this data a look using vanilla `{leaflet}`:

```{r map-basic}
port_talbot$open_year <- as.integer(format(port_talbot$start_date, "%Y"))

port_talbot$popup <-
  paste0(
    "<strong>",
    toupper(port_talbot$site),
    "</strong> (",
    port_talbot$code,
    ")<hr>Site Type: ",
    port_talbot$site_type,
    "<br>Opened: ",
    port_talbot$open_year
  )

leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(popup = ~popup)
```

# Simple Example

We can use the `magicIcons()` function to swap out the default markers for some `{leaf.magic}` markers. The important argument here is `icon`, which is the (in this case) Font Awesome icon of interest^[See `fontawesome::fa_metadata()` for a complete list].

```{r map-simple}
leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(
    popup = ~popup,
    icon = magicIcons(
      icon = "cloud"
    )
  )
```

# Icon Libraries

By default, `magicIcons()` uses Font Awesome icons, but the `library` argument lets you choose from four icon libraries. Each is provided by a different package, which you'll need to have installed to use it:

| `library` | Icons | Package |
|---|---|---|
| `"fontawesome"` | <https://fontawesome.com/search?ic=free> | `{fontawesome}` |
| `"bootstrap"` | <https://icons.getbootstrap.com/> | `{bsicons}` |
| `"lucide"` | <https://lucide.dev/icons/> | `{lucidr}` |
| `"ionicons"` | <https://ionic.io/ionicons> | None - icons are downloaded when first used, so require an internet connection |

For example, here are some Lucide icons:

```{r map-library}
leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(
    popup = ~popup,
    icon = magicIcons(
      icon = "factory",
      library = "lucide"
    )
  )
```

# Varying Icons

`{leaf.magic}` allows you to vary icons by some other variable. You can do this manually, or use one of `{leaf.magic}` constructor functions like `iconFactor()`.

```{r map-varicon}
site_types <- c("Urban Industrial", "Urban Background", "Urban Traffic")

# like leaflet::colorFactor(), levels are sorted alphabetically:
# "Urban Background", "Urban Industrial", "Urban Traffic"
iconPal <- iconFactor(
  icons = c("house", "industry", "car"),
  domain = site_types
)

leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(
    popup = ~popup,
    icon = ~ magicIcons(
      icon = iconPal(site_type)
    )
  )
```

Note that there's also `iconBin()` and `iconQuantile()` which can help map icons to numeric data. In this case, it makes most sense to choose icons that have some inherent "order" to them.

These functions take the same arguments as `colorFactor()`, `colorBin()` and `colorQuantile()` and split the data in exactly the same way, so if you give an icon function and a colour function the same settings (and the same number of icons as colours), every level gets a consistent icon-colour pair. They are also icon-led - the `bins` and `n` arguments default to the length of the provided `icons`, so you don't need to specify them if you're happy letting the functions decide the break-points/`probs` for you.

```{r map-varicon-q}
iconPalYr <- iconQuantile(
  icons = c("hourglass-start", "hourglass-half", "hourglass-end"),
  domain = port_talbot$open_year
)

leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(
    popup = ~popup,
    icon = ~ magicIcons(
      icon = iconPalYr(open_year)
    )
  )
```

# Varying Colours

`magicIcons()` has two arguments related to colour; `markerColor` which colours the marker, and `iconColor` which colours the icon. Any colour can be supplied to these arguments - either a constant value or colour values mapped to a column using, for example, `leaflet::colorFactor()`.

```{r map-varcol-fct}
catPal <- colorFactor(c("#12436D", "#28A197", "#801650"), port_talbot$site_type)

leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(
    popup = ~popup,
    icon = ~ magicIcons(
      icon = iconPal(site_type),
      markerColor = catPal(site_type),
      iconColor = "#F7F7F7FF"
    )
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    pal = catPal,
    values = port_talbot$site_type,
    title = "Site Type"
  )
```

As the markers themselves can be set to *any* colour, we can even use a continuous scale (e.g., from `leaflet::colorNumeric()`).

```{r map-varcol-num}
palNum <- colorNumeric("viridis", domain = port_talbot$open_year)

leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(
    popup = ~popup,
    icon = ~ magicIcons(
      icon = iconPalYr(open_year),
      markerColor = palNum(open_year),
      iconColor = "white"
    )
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    pal = palNum,
    values = port_talbot$open_year,
    title = "Opening Year",
    labFormat = labelFormat(big.mark = "")
  )
```

# Varying Size

Unlike `leaflet::awesomeIcons()`, `magicIcons()` can be easily re-sized. Much like in `leaflet::addCircleMarkers()`, this can vary with another variable; let's make the closed sites a bit smaller than the open ones with `markerSize`, which sets the width of the marker in pixels. Note the default is `30L`, which is roughly the same size as the default `leaflet::addMarkers()` marker.

```{r map-varsize}
leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(
    popup = ~popup,
    icon = ~ magicIcons(
      icon = iconPal(site_type),
      iconColor = "white",
      markerSize = ifelse(open, 30L, 20L),
      markerColor = catPal(site_type)
    )
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    pal = catPal,
    values = port_talbot$site_type,
    title = "Site Type"
  )
```

# Icon Legends

`{leaf.magic}` provides the `addIconLegend()` function to construct icon legends. It works just like `leaflet::addLegend()`: give it an icon scale as `pal` along with the `values` used on the map, and it works out the icons and labels for you.

```{r map-iconlegend}
leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(
    popup = ~popup,
    icon = ~ magicIcons(
      icon = iconPal(site_type),
      markerColor = palNum(open_year),
      iconColor = "white"
    )
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    pal = palNum,
    values = port_talbot$open_year,
    title = "Opening Year",
    labFormat = labelFormat(big.mark = "")
  ) |>
  addIconLegend(
    pal = iconPal,
    values = ~site_type,
    title = "Site Type"
  )
```

Often, the colour of the marker (or icon) and the icon itself will align. In that case, a colour scale can be passed to the `colors` argument of `addIconLegend()` to create an efficient, combined legend. As long as the icon and colour scales share the same settings, every icon is paired with the right colour.

```{r map-iconcollegend}
leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(
    popup = ~popup,
    icon = ~ magicIcons(
      icon = iconPal(site_type),
      iconColor = "white",
      markerColor = catPal(site_type)
    )
  ) |>
  addIconLegend(
    pal = iconPal,
    values = ~site_type,
    colors = catPal,
    title = "Site Type"
  )
```

This also works for numeric scales; for example, an `iconQuantile()` scale gives one legend item per quantile.

```{r map-iconlegend-q}
# colorQuantile() defaults to n = 4, so match the 3 icons of iconPalYr
colPalYr <- colorQuantile(
  c("#12436D", "#28A197", "#801650"),
  domain = port_talbot$open_year,
  n = 3
)

leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(
    popup = ~popup,
    icon = ~ magicIcons(
      icon = iconPalYr(open_year),
      iconColor = "white",
      markerColor = colPalYr(open_year)
    )
  ) |>
  addIconLegend(
    pal = iconPalYr,
    values = ~open_year,
    colors = colPalYr,
    title = "Opening Year"
  )
```

Legends can also be built by hand with the `icons`, `labels` and `colors` arguments, and - like `leaflet::addLegend()` - shown and hidden alongside a layer using `group`.

```{r map-iconlegend-manual}
leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(
    popup = ~popup,
    icon = ~ magicIcons(
      icon = iconPal(site_type),
      iconColor = "white",
      markerColor = catPal(site_type)
    ),
    group = "Sites"
  ) |>
  addIconLegend(
    icons = c("industry", "car", "house"),
    labels = c("Industrial", "Traffic", "Background"),
    colors = c("#28A197", "#801650", "#12436D"),
    title = "Site Type",
    group = "Sites"
  ) |>
  addLayersControl(
    overlayGroups = "Sites",
    options = layersControlOptions(FALSE)
  )
```

# Marker Shapes

While the default marker type, the "tear-drop" marker, is useful in most instances, you may find other marker shapes of interest. These are:

* **Pointed shapes**, which sit on their location with their tip, like the default marker: `"marker"`, `"marker-square"` (a pin with a square head) and `"callout"` (a speech bubble).

* **Centred shapes**, which sit centred on their location: `"circle"`, `"square"`, `"diamond"`, `"triangle"`, `"hexagon"`, `"star"` and `"heart"`.

* `"none"`, which removes the marker entirely and places the icon directly on the map itself.

Use the layer control in the map below to try them out.

```{r map-shapes}
shapes <- c(
  "marker", "marker-square", "callout", "circle", "square", "diamond",
  "triangle", "hexagon", "star", "heart", "none"
)

addQuickMarker <- function(map, marker) {
  iconColor <- "white"
  markerColor <- catPal(port_talbot$site_type)
  if (marker == "none") {
    iconColor <- markerColor
  }
  map |>
    addMarkers(
      popup = ~ popup,
      icon = ~ magicIcons(
        icon = iconPal(site_type),
        iconColor = iconColor,
        markerColor = markerColor,
        marker = marker
      ),
      group = marker
    )
}

map <- leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles()

for (shape in shapes) {
  map <- addQuickMarker(map, shape)
}

map |>
  addLayersControl(
    baseGroups = shapes,
    options = layersControlOptions(FALSE)
  ) |>
  addIconLegend(
    position = "bottomleft",
    pal = iconPal,
    values = ~site_type,
    colors = catPal,
    title = "Site Type"
  )
```

Note that `marker` can vary with some variable, allowing the marker shape itself to encode extra information. As marker shapes are just names, `iconFactor()` can map data to them.

```{r map-shapes-vary}
markPal <- iconFactor(c("circle", "diamond", "square"), site_types)

leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(icon = ~ magicIcons(
    marker = markPal(site_type),
    markerSize = ifelse(markPal(site_type) == "diamond", 35, 30)
  )) |>
  addIconLegend(
    pal = markPal,
    values = ~site_type,
    title = "Site Type"
  )
```

## Custom Shapes

If none of the built-in shapes suit, you can design your own with `markerShape()`. A shape is drawn with SVG in its own coordinate system - by default, 100 units wide and 100 units tall - and you tell `markerShape()`:

* `path`: the outline of the shape, as SVG path data or SVG markup.
* `icon`: the centre (`x`, `y`) and `size` of the square the icon is drawn in.
* `anchor`: the point of the shape that sits on the marker's location.
* `popup`: where popups open from.

The shape is filled with `markerColor` and given a darker outline for you. For example, here's a downward-pointing arrow, anchored at its tip:

```{r shape-arrow}
arrow <- markerShape(
  path = "M2 2h96L50 98z",
  icon = c(x = 50, y = 34, size = 36),
  anchor = c(x = 50, y = 98),
  popup = c(x = 50, y = 10),
  shadow = "cast"
)

arrow
```

A custom shape can be passed to `marker` just like a built-in one. To use a different shape for each marker, give `marker` a list of shapes and/or shape names. Here, open sites use the arrow and closed sites use a circle.

```{r map-shape-custom}
leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(
    popup = ~popup,
    icon = ~ magicIcons(
      icon = iconPal(site_type),
      iconColor = "white",
      markerColor = catPal(site_type),
      marker = lapply(open, \(x) if (x) arrow else "circle")
    )
  ) |>
  addIconLegend(
    pal = iconPal,
    values = ~site_type,
    colors = catPal,
    title = "Site Type"
  )
```

# Shadows

Like the default `{leaflet}` marker, `{leaf.magic}` markers have shadows. Pointed shapes cast a shadow up and to the right from their tip, as if they were standing on the map, while other shapes have a soft shadow just beneath them. Shadows are drawn underneath *all* of the markers, so a marker's shadow never covers another marker.

Shadows can be turned off with `shadow = FALSE`. Use the layer control below to compare. For custom shapes, the `shadow` argument of `markerShape()` chooses between a `"cast"` shadow, a `"drop"` shadow, or `"none"`.

```{r map-shadows}
addShadowMarkers <- function(map, shadow) {
  map |>
    addMarkers(
      popup = ~popup,
      icon = ~ magicIcons(
        icon = iconPal(site_type),
        iconColor = "white",
        markerColor = catPal(site_type),
        shadow = shadow
      ),
      group = if (shadow) "With Shadows" else "Without Shadows"
    )
}

leaflet(port_talbot) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addShadowMarkers(TRUE) |>
  addShadowMarkers(FALSE) |>
  addLayersControl(
    baseGroups = c("With Shadows", "Without Shadows"),
    options = layersControlOptions(FALSE)
  )
```

# Other Utilities

`{leaf.magic}` exports the `awesomePalette` list, which are hex codes for the colours used in `leaflet::awesomeIcons()`. You could use these if you want to recreate the colour scheme of `awesomeIcons()` with the flexibility of `magicIcons()`.

```{r awesomepal}
cols <- names(awesomePalette)[names(awesomePalette) != "white"]

breweries91$facolor <- sample(cols, nrow(breweries91), replace = TRUE)

breweries91$hexcolor <- unlist(use.names = FALSE, awesomePalette[breweries91$facolor])

leaflet(breweries91) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addAwesomeMarkers(
    icon = ~ awesomeIcons(
      icon = "circle",
      markerColor = facolor,
      iconColor = "#FFFFFF",
      library = "fa"
    ),
    group = "Awesome"
  ) |>
  addMarkers(
    icon = ~ magicIcons(
      icon = "fas fa-circle",
      markerColor = hexcolor,
      iconColor = "#FFFFFF"
    ),
    group = "Magic"
  ) |>
  addLayersControl(
    baseGroups = c("Awesome", "Magic")
  )
```

If you use `{leaf.magic}`, you may want to add an attribution to Font Awesome or one of the other icon providers (set using `library`). `addIconAttribution()` is a convenient way to do this, and even comes with its own `group` and `layerId` options for precise "layer" control. Try toggling the breweries on and off in the example below.

```{r attribution}
leaflet(breweries91) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addMarkers(icon = magicIcons("beer", "red", "white"), group = "Breweries") |>
  addIconAttribution(group = "Breweries") |>
  addLayersControl(overlayGroups = "Breweries",
                   options = leaflet::layersControlOptions(FALSE))
```

Finally, markers are saved to a temporary directory by default, which is cleared at the end of each R session. If you build the same markers often (for example, in a Shiny app), the `dir` argument of `magicIcons()` can point to a permanent directory so that markers are only ever built once.
